variants.title: Run the update cycle
variants.context: A continual-learning update runs as a cycle: detect meaningful change, curate an update set that mixes recent data with retained knowledge, adapt under constraints that protect prior parameters, evaluate the new task and the retained tasks together, then release reversibly.
variants.prompt: A deployed model starts seeing a new pattern in production. Put the continual-learning steps in order.

items.text: Build the update set by combining recent examples with a bounded replay sample or another preservation mechanism.
Test transfer and forgetting by measuring the new task, retained tasks, backward transfer, latency, and memory cost together.
Release reversibly by canarying the update, retaining rollback artifacts, and continuing to monitor the triggering distribution.
Adapt under constraints so regularization, memory, or modular structure protects prior knowledge while parameters move.
Detect meaningful change and separate persistent drift or a new task from noise, seasonality, and instrumentation failures.

variants.hint: Which step decides whether there is anything real to learn from?
variants.explanation: Adaptation is only safe once the change is real, the update set preserves history, and both new and retained tasks pass their gates.

variants.title: Run the update cycle
variants.context: A continual-learning update runs as a cycle: detect meaningful change, curate an update set that mixes recent data with retained knowledge, adapt under constraints that protect prior parameters, evaluate the new task and the retained tasks together, then release reversibly.
variants.prompt: A team wants a single update to add a new label without losing old ones. Put the work in order.

items.text: Assemble a batch that mixes new-label examples with replay coverage of the existing labels.
Confirm the new label reflects a persistent change rather than a short instrumentation gap.
Ship behind a canary with the previous checkpoint retained as the rollback target.
Score the new label and every previously learned label from the same checkpoint.
Fine-tune with the preservation mechanism active so shared parameters are not rewritten freely.

variants.hint: The batch composition is decided before any gradient step is taken.
variants.explanation: Replay coverage has to be in the batch itself, because a preservation mechanism cannot protect classes the update never revisits.

variants.title: Run the update cycle
variants.context: A continual-learning update runs as a cycle: detect meaningful change, curate an update set that mixes recent data with retained knowledge, adapt under constraints that protect prior parameters, evaluate the new task and the retained tasks together, then release reversibly.
variants.prompt: An adaptation shipped last month and the triggering distribution is still moving. Put the follow-up steps in order.

items.text: Canary the new checkpoint while the previous one stays serving and reversible.
Rebuild the update set so retained tasks keep bounded coverage alongside the newest window.
Re-detect the change against the monitoring set to confirm the movement persisted after the last update.
Adapt again under the same constraints, versioning the buffer and data window with the model.
Re-run the task-by-time evaluation to see whether the second update eroded the first one's gains.

variants.hint: Each pass through the cycle produces a new row in the task-by-time matrix.
variants.explanation: Continual learning evaluates the sequence rather than the latest model, so every update re-scores every task seen so far.

variants.title: Keep the update reversible
variants.context: A drift alert is evidence to investigate, not permission to retrain. A production policy diagnoses the cause, validates labels and contracts, evaluates retained tasks, canaries the update, and keeps the prior checkpoint and a tested traffic rollback available throughout.
variants.prompt: A drift monitor fires on a live model and an engineer wants to retrain today. Put the policy steps in order.

items.text: Evaluate the candidate on the new distribution and on every protected retained task.
Promote broadly only after retained-task gates and canary metrics both hold.
Diagnose the cause and rule out seasonality, noise, and instrumentation failure.
Canary the update on a traffic slice while the prior checkpoint stays loaded.
Validate that labels and input contracts for the new window can be trusted.
Build the update set from the validated window plus bounded replay of retained tasks.

variants.hint: What has to be ruled out before a single statistic is allowed to trigger training?
variants.explanation: A single drift statistic must not trigger an irreversible update, so diagnosis and label validation come before any training run.

variants.title: Keep the update reversible
variants.context: A drift alert is evidence to investigate, not permission to retrain. A production policy diagnoses the cause, validates labels and contracts, evaluates retained tasks, canaries the update, and keeps the prior checkpoint and a tested traffic rollback available throughout.
variants.prompt: A canary improves the new task but regresses a protected historical slice. Put the recovery steps in order.

items.text: Confirm the restored checkpoint runs with its compatible feature schema and buffer version.
Diagnose which part of the update overwrote the protected behavior before trying again.
Route traffic back to the retained prior checkpoint using the tested rollback path.
Stop expanding the canary and hold traffic at its current share.
Catch the regression from the retained-task evaluation running against canary traffic.

variants.hint: The point of a canary is that the blast radius is still small when the evidence arrives.
variants.explanation: Rollback is part of continual learning rather than a separate deployment detail, which is why the prior checkpoint and its features are retained.

variants.title: Keep the update reversible
variants.context: A drift alert is evidence to investigate, not permission to retrain. A production policy diagnoses the cause, validates labels and contracts, evaluates retained tasks, canaries the update, and keeps the prior checkpoint and a tested traffic rollback available throughout.
variants.prompt: Labels for the new distribution become unreliable while automatic adaptation is running. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the current model version, replay buffer, data window, and task definition together.
Resume adaptation only with a canary and a tested rollback in place.
Repair the label or input contract before any further update set is built.
Re-run the retained-task evaluation to confirm nothing already shipped has regressed.
Stop automatic adaptation as soon as the label or contract signal is untrustworthy.

variants.hint: An automatic loop fed by bad labels learns the defect faster than a human can catch it.
variants.explanation: Automatic adaptation is stopped when labels, input contracts, or monitoring signals are unreliable, because the loop would otherwise encode the failure.

variants.title: Name the learning scenario
variants.context: Three scenarios need different designs. Task-incremental learning knows the task identity at inference and can route to a task head. Domain-incremental learning keeps the task and labels while the input domain moves. Class-incremental learning expands the label set and cannot assume which class group a request belongs to.
variants.prompt: A sentiment model trained on electronics reviews must now handle grocery reviews. The labels are unchanged and no domain tag is supplied at inference time. Which scenario is this?
options: Domain-incremental learning, because the input distribution moved under a fixed label set.
Task-incremental learning, because a second review source is a second task.
Class-incremental learning, because grocery reviews expand what the model must recognize.
optionFeedback: Correct: the task and labels stay the same while the environment changes, with no domain label at inference.
Task-incremental learning requires the task identity to be known at request time, which is not available here.
No new labels were added; the same sentiment classes apply to both review sources.
variants.hint: Ask two questions: did the label set grow, and is the identity known at inference time?
variants.explanation: Domain-incremental learning keeps the task fixed while the input domain moves, so the model cannot rely on a routing signal.

variants.title: Name the learning scenario
variants.context: Three scenarios need different designs. Task-incremental learning knows the task identity at inference and can route to a task head. Domain-incremental learning keeps the task and labels while the input domain moves. Class-incremental learning expands the label set and cannot assume which class group a request belongs to.
variants.prompt: One model family adds a detection capability after classification, and every caller states which capability it is invoking. Which scenario is this?
options: Domain-incremental learning, because the inputs now include new imagery.
Task-incremental learning, because task identity is known and each request can be routed to its head.
Class-incremental learning, because the output space grew.
optionFeedback: The task itself changed, so this is not a fixed task over a moving input domain.
Correct: a stated task identity lets the system route to the appropriate task head.
The two capabilities are distinct tasks with their own heads, not new classes inside one head.
variants.hint: Whether a routing signal exists at inference time changes the design more than the number of outputs does.
variants.explanation: Task-incremental learning is the easiest of the three because the known task identity removes the need to discriminate across task groups.

variants.title: Name the learning scenario
variants.context: Three scenarios need different designs. Task-incremental learning knows the task identity at inference and can route to a task head. Domain-incremental learning keeps the task and labels while the input domain moves. Class-incremental learning expands the label set and cannot assume which class group a request belongs to.
variants.prompt: A wildlife classifier must recognize five newly catalogued species while still recognizing every earlier species, and a photo arrives with no hint about which group it belongs to. Which scenario is this?
options: Class-incremental learning, because the label set expanded with no group hint at inference.
Domain-incremental learning, because new cameras changed the imagery.
Task-incremental learning, because each species group is its own task.
optionFeedback: Correct: new classes arrive while old classes must still be recognized, with no group signal.
The label set itself grew, which is more than a moving input domain.
No task identity is supplied, so the model cannot route the photo to a species-group head.
variants.hint: The hard part is deciding across old and new labels at once.
variants.explanation: Class-incremental learning is the hardest of the three because the model must discriminate across the whole expanded label set without a group hint.

variants.title: Match the preservation mechanism
variants.context: Four preservation mechanisms trade different costs. Replay stores or generates old examples. Regularization such as EWC penalizes movement of parameters important to earlier tasks. Task-specific modules add adapters or heads instead of rewriting shared parameters. Distillation preserves the previous model's outputs on retained inputs.
variants.prompt: Match each preservation mechanism to how it protects earlier knowledge.

pairs.label: Experience replay
pairs.detail: Mixes stored or generated old examples into each update batch.

pairs.label: Regularization such as EWC
pairs.detail: Penalizes movement of parameters judged important to earlier tasks.

pairs.label: Task-specific modules
pairs.detail: Adds adapters, heads, or columns instead of rewriting shared parameters.

pairs.label: Distillation
pairs.detail: Trains the new model to reproduce the previous model's outputs on retained inputs.

variants.hint: Ask what each mechanism actually stores: examples, parameter importances, structure, or behavior.
variants.explanation: The mechanisms differ in what they preserve, which is why their costs land on memory, importance estimates, model size, or inherited behavior.

variants.title: Match the preservation mechanism
variants.context: Four preservation mechanisms trade different costs. Replay stores or generates old examples. Regularization such as EWC penalizes movement of parameters important to earlier tasks. Task-specific modules add adapters or heads instead of rewriting shared parameters. Distillation preserves the previous model's outputs on retained inputs.
variants.prompt: Match each preservation mechanism to the cost it imposes on the system.

pairs.label: Experience replay
pairs.detail: Memory policy and privacy constraints become part of the model design.

pairs.label: Regularization such as EWC
pairs.detail: Importance estimates get less reliable across long task sequences.

pairs.label: Task-specific modules
pairs.detail: Model size and routing complexity grow with every added task.

pairs.label: Distillation
pairs.detail: Old mistakes are preserved along with the behavior worth keeping.

variants.hint: Every mechanism buys stability with a different currency.
variants.explanation: Choosing a mechanism means accepting its cost, so the decision depends on memory limits, sequence length, size budget, and how good the incumbent actually is.

variants.title: Match the preservation mechanism
variants.context: Four preservation mechanisms trade different costs. Replay stores or generates old examples. Regularization such as EWC penalizes movement of parameters important to earlier tasks. Task-specific modules add adapters or heads instead of rewriting shared parameters. Distillation preserves the previous model's outputs on retained inputs.
variants.prompt: Match each constraint to the preservation mechanism it favors.

pairs.label: Raw user examples cannot be retained
pairs.detail: Penalize parameter movement instead of storing data.

pairs.label: Serving size and routing budget are generous
pairs.detail: Add a module per task so interference stays low.

pairs.label: Retained labels are missing but the incumbent is trusted
pairs.detail: Match the previous model's outputs on retained inputs.

pairs.label: Memory is available and tasks are close together
pairs.detail: Mix a bounded sample of old examples into every batch.

variants.hint: Start from what the constraint forbids, then pick the mechanism that does not need it.
variants.explanation: The constraint usually picks the mechanism, because replay needs data, distillation needs a trusted incumbent, and modules need size budget.

variants.title: Read the task-by-time matrix
variants.context: Continual-learning evaluation uses a task-by-time matrix: after each update, every task seen so far is scored. Forgetting is an earlier task's best historical score minus its score after later updates, and average accuracy covers every task seen so far, not only the newest one.
variants.prompt: Task A reached 91 percent after the update that taught it, and scores 78 percent after two later updates. What is the forgetting on task A?
variants.hint: Forgetting compares a task against its own historical best, not against the newest task.
variants.explanation: Forgetting is the earlier task's best historical score minus its current score, here 91 minus 78.

mistakes.feedback: That is the current score; forgetting is the drop from the historical best.
That is the historical best; forgetting is the difference between the two scores.

variants.title: Read the task-by-time matrix
variants.context: Continual-learning evaluation uses a task-by-time matrix: after each update, every task seen so far is scored. Forgetting is an earlier task's best historical score minus its score after later updates, and average accuracy covers every task seen so far, not only the newest one.
variants.prompt: After the third update, the three tasks seen so far score 88, 74, and 96 percent. What is the average accuracy?
variants.hint: Average accuracy covers every task seen so far, not the newest one.
variants.explanation: Average accuracy is the mean over all tasks seen so far, here 258 divided by 3, which exposes gains bought by erasing earlier capability.

mistakes.feedback: That is the newest task alone, which is exactly the metric this one replaces.
That is the sum of the scores; divide by the number of tasks.

variants.title: Read the task-by-time matrix
variants.context: Continual-learning evaluation uses a task-by-time matrix: after each update, every task seen so far is scored. Forgetting is an earlier task's best historical score minus its score after later updates, and average accuracy covers every task seen so far, not only the newest one.
variants.prompt: After update 4 the retained tasks score 70 percent (best 90), 82 percent (best 85), and 87 percent (best 88). The newest task scores 94 percent. What is the average forgetting across the retained tasks?
variants.hint: Only tasks with an earlier best can be forgotten.
variants.explanation: Average forgetting is the mean of 20, 3, and 1 over the three retained tasks, which shows most of the damage sits in one task.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by four, but the newest task has no earlier best to forget from.
That is the worst single task's forgetting rather than the average across retained tasks.
